nameStory: Sweet alyssum gets its delightful name from its incredibly fragrant flowers that smell like honey mixed with vanilla. The word 'alyssum' comes from the Greek words meaning 'without madness' - ancient Greeks believed this plant could cure rabies and calm anger. When you catch a whiff of its sweet perfume on a summer evening, you'll understand why gardeners have treasured it for centuries.
description: Sweet alyssum is a low-growing annual flower that forms dense, spreading mats covered in tiny four-petaled blooms. These charming little plants typically grow only 4-6 inches tall but can spread 6-12 inches wide, creating carpet-like patches. The flowers are usually white but can also be pink, purple, or pale yellow, and they're packed so densely that they often completely hide the small, narrow leaves beneath. Originally from the Mediterranean, sweet alyssum has become a beloved garden plant that sometimes escapes cultivation in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny four-petaled flowers less than 1/4 inch across, packed into dense, rounded clusters that smell intensely sweet and honey-like - you can often smell them before you see them

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, rarely growing taller than 6 inches but spreading outward in dense carpets

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel slightly fuzzy and are often hidden beneath the profusion of flowers

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny oval seed pods that are flattened and papery when mature, splitting open to release very small round seeds

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bloom continuously from spring until hard frost, with flower clusters becoming more numerous and fragrant in cool weather

habitat: Sweet alyssum thrives in disturbed soils, garden edges, sidewalk cracks, and areas with well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun to partial shade. In New England, you'll most commonly find it as a garden escapee near homes, in abandoned lots, along pathways, and in other human-disturbed areas. It prefers cooler temperatures and actually performs better in New England's climate than in hot, humid regions.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin blooming in late spring, forming small mats with the first flush of intensely fragrant white flowers.
seasonality.summer: Continues blooming through summer but may slow down during the hottest weeks, then rebounds with cooler weather and increased fragrance.
seasonality.fall: Reaches peak bloom and fragrance in early fall, producing masses of flowers until the first hard frost kills the plants.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only dried brown stems and scattered seeds that will germinate the following spring.

funFact: Sweet alyssum flowers actually become MORE fragrant in cool weather and at night - the plant pumps out extra perfume when temperatures drop to attract the moths and other nighttime pollinators that are most active in cooler conditions.
confusionNotes: Sweet alyssum's tiny white flowers might be confused with baby's breath, but baby's breath grows much taller (2-3 feet), has a more open, airy flower structure, and lacks the intense honey fragrance. Remember: if it smells like candy and hugs the ground, it's sweet alyssum!
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name, sweet alyssum isn't actually in the true Alyssum genus anymore - botanists moved it to Lobularia, though gardeners and seed packets still call it alyssum. This naming confusion is common in the mustard family, where many plants have been reclassified as genetic studies reveal their true relationships.
compareHints: Sweet alyssum is the only Lobularia species commonly found in New England. Among other small white-flowered mustard family plants, it's distinguished by its incredibly low, mat-forming growth habit and intense fragrance. Most other mustard family members grow more upright and lack the sweet honey scent that makes alyssum so distinctive.
